vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his shoulders drawn inward, his uniform still damp from the morning's training exercises. At thirty-seven, he carries himself with the careful posture of someone who has learned to take up less space, to be less visible. His wife Layla made him come today. He didn't want to.

Five years ago, Marcus was a different man. He loved his job-the camaraderie at the station, the clarity of purpose, the way his team depended on him. He was confident then, quick with jokes, the kind of guy who'd volunteer for extra shifts. He and Layla had just bought their house. Life felt solid.

Then came the calls. A woman named Diane, someone he'd met briefly at a community event where he'd given a fire safety presentation. She called the station asking for him specifically. When he politely declined to take her calls, she began showing up-at the grocery store where he shopped, outside the station during his shifts, at the park near his house where he jogged. She sent letters. She called their home at three in the morning. Marcus reported it to the police, filed a restraining order, but the months stretched on. The unpredictability was suffocating. He never knew when he'd turn a corner and find her there.

The worst came eighteen months into it. Marcus came home to find Diane inside his house, having somehow gotten past the locked door. She was sitting in his living room. His heart nearly stopped. He called 911 from outside, and she was arrested, but something inside him fractured that day.

Now, five years later, Marcus is a ghost of himself. He takes the same route to the station every day because deviating from routine makes his chest tight and his hands shake. He no longer goes to the grocery store-Layla does all the shopping. He quit jogging. He stopped attending the Friday night dinners with his crew, making excuses about fatigue, though everyone knows something changed.

At the station, Marcus performs his duties adequately, but his commanding officer has noticed he's withdrawn. He doesn't participate in the usual banter. When the alarm sounds, Marcus responds, but there's a brittleness to him now. Last month, during a routine call to a house fire, he froze for a critical moment when he saw a woman watching from the crowd outside. It wasn't Diane-it was someone who merely resembled her-but his body didn't know the difference. His hands trembled as he operated the equipment. A younger firefighter had to cover for him.

At home, Layla watches her husband disappear into himself each evening. He checks the locks multiple times before bed. He keeps the curtains drawn. He startles at unexpected sounds. When she touches him without warning, he flinches. They haven't been intimate in three years. She's tried to talk to him about it, but Marcus insists he's fine, that he's just tired. He tells her the job is demanding. He tells her nothing is wrong.

But something is profoundly wrong, and Marcus knows it. He's hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. His mind generates threats constantly-in parking lots, in crowds, in the faces of strangers. The violation of his home, of his sanctuary, lives in his body as a permanent state of alarm. He wonders if he can keep doing this job, if he can keep being the man everyone needs him to be, when he feels like he's barely holding together.
